dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Thorough reverse-engineering: read problem.py, reference kernel, tests; used inspect.getsource on Machine/step/all engines; correctly extracted SLOT_LIMITS, VLEN=8, parallel-engine cost model, no-intra-cycle-forwarding, and the reference forest/hash/index computation.

Wrote Python simulations of the reference algorithm to probe index distribution per round (indices reset after round 10, per-round distinct-index counts) — experiment-driven orientation beyond static reading.
Repeatedly discovered/confirmed the no-forwarding data hazard via debugging (write-then-read in same bundle), refining the operational model of bundle semantics.

The core VLIW cost-model insight (all engines execute concurrently per bundle) was 're-realized' multiple times rather than grasped up front, indicating the operational model wasn't cleanly internalized early.
Flip-flopped on the exact reference contract (whether positional element ordering permits sorted grouping), showing an incomplete/churning grasp of the semantics the kernel must satisfy.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well past level 5: it read problem.py and the reference kernel, used inspection to pull the full ISA, correctly identified ops, per-bundle cost, SLOT_LIMITS, SIMD width, no-forwarding, and the computation, and it probed the simulator with algorithm simulations and repeated debugging (level-8 behaviors like hash-stage dependency and no-forwarding confirmation). It stops short of a clean 8/10 because the operational model had recurring gaps — the VLIW packing cost model was re-derived multiple times and the reference ordering contract was misunderstood repeatedly rather than continuously and cleanly refined. That places it at a strong 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates

evidence.note: Repeated explicit per-stage cycle estimates mapped to the 1250 budget and to the machine's real bottlenecks (LOAD vs VALU), showing a sensible ordered plan with rough per-stage targets — the substance of the level-5 anchor and reaching toward budget-mapping.

Actual landed-and-measured milestones (5,130 then 8,018 then 11,602 cycles) with cycle deltas attributed to specific transforms (2-way interleave, scratch-resident), demonstrating checkpoints per stage.

Repeated collapse of the ladder: agent abandons aggressive transforms after correctness/scratch failures and reverts to 'the simple working kernel', showing milestones were not independently revertible/measurable and correctness+speed changes were entangled — well short of the level-8 anchor.
Long stretch of restating the same 'sorted grouping + 4-way + multiply_add' plan without landing it; heavy planning ceremony and circling rather than sequenced, evidence-driven decomposition.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has a genuinely sensible ordered plan with rough per-stage cycle targets and bottleneck-aware budget estimates (matching and slightly exceeding the level-5 anchor via quantitative per-stage mapping). But it fails the level-8 requirement that transforms be sequenced as independently measurable and revertible correctness-preserving steps: it repeatedly entangled correctness and speed in wholesale rewrites, broke correctness, and fell back to a known-good kernel, so the milestone structure existed more in restated intent than in disciplined execution. This lands it squarely at 5.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test

evidence.note: Runs run_tests.sh repeatedly after significant changes, confirming both correctness and cycle count and re-checking after each optimization stage (solid level-5 baseline behavior).
Runs the unittest CorrectnessTests suite directly, and notes small test passes but full benchmark fails — distinguishing canonical vs broader correctness rather than trusting one pass.

Builds self-constructed Python simulations of the reference algorithm (distinct-index counting, verifying sorted-order/even-odd partition preserves results) as additional checks beyond the provided test — a level-8 behavior; but some sims had their own unresolved bugs, limiting rigor.
Isolates transforms with minimal 1-vector/1-round tests, comparing scratch state at every step against reference computation to localize divergence — transform-level correctness isolation.

Repeatedly detects and fixes VLIW-specific hazards (intra-cycle no-forwarding writes corrupting state) surfaced through testing — guarding against the specific ways VLIW scheduling corrupts state (level-10 flavored, but caught reactively via debugging rather than a systematic guard).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it re-runs run_tests.sh and unittest after stages, confirms both correctness and cycles, and does not treat a single canonical pass as proof. It reaches into anchor 8 by building self-generated reference comparisons (Python sims of the algorithm) and isolating transforms with tiny 1-vector tests, and it repeatedly catches VLIW-specific state-corruption hazards. However, verification is applied inconsistently amid heavy kernel-rewrite thrash and some self-built checks were themselves buggy, so it falls short of the disciplined, systematic regime of 8-10. That places it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection

evidence.note: Early on, tracks descending cycle counts (16,973 → 14,157 → 13,645) and repeatedly states distance to the 1250 target — genuine history-keeping of measured numbers.

Cites 'current best' figures and attributes them to transforms (2-way interleave → 8,018 '18x'; scratch-resident → 11,602), meeting anchor-5 tracking, but never improves past 8,018 and cannot reliably reproduce it.

Severe circular debugging: repeatedly reverts to 'the simple working kernel' (13,906), re-attempts the same grouping/uniformity/4-way approaches, and rediscovers identical bugs (data hazards, load-slot & scratch overflow). Verbally notes being 'stuck' (133) but keeps grinding the same exhausted line instead of redirecting.
Explicitly recognizes the stall ('We're stuck at 13,906', 'spent a lot of time') yet fails to reallocate effort — the hallmark gap versus anchor 8's redirect-instead-of-grind behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably tracks measured cycle counts, knows its distance to the 1250 target, and roughly attributes gains to specific transforms — squarely meeting anchor 5's tracking criteria. However, it exhibits pronounced circling: dozens of full rewrites re-trying the same grouping/interleaving approaches and rediscovering the same bugs, and it never builds a transform→delta ledger nor redirects after recognizing plateaus (it grinds the same exhausted approach), and even loses reproducibility of its best correct kernel. That mix of solid number-tracking with heavy, unrecovered thrash places it between anchors 3 and 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead

evidence.note: Repeatedly diagnoses the SAME class of correctness break — data hazards from no intra-cycle forwarding (multiply+add or XOR+parity in one bundle reading stale values) — and correctly splits ops into separate cycles. Genuine machine-model correction when surprised.

Discovers the uniformity-check optimization is invalid without sorted data (idx[0]==idx[VLEN-1] doesn't imply all equal), backs it out multiple times. Updates understanding rather than entrenching a broken assumption.

Cleanly reverts to the last known-correct kernel (11,602 / 13,906) after complex interleaved versions fail correctness, preserving hard-won working state — the level-5 'back it out and try a different tactic' behavior.

Sunk-cost/flailing signal: hits 'Out of scratch space' with double-buffered sorted arrays repeatedly, each time says 'keep data in memory', yet re-attempts the same scratch-heavy grouping approach again — the falsified constraint is not internalized decisively.

Declares 'BREAKTHROUGH: sorted grouping is correct!' several times, then keeps circling back to it despite repeated implementation failures; oscillates between 2-way and 4-way interleaving without a decisive pivot — flailing that keeps it below the level-8 anchor.
Correctly recognizes that grouping/reordering elements breaks the positional correctness test, abandoning the invalid transform — a real correction, though later partially re-litigated.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly clears anchor 5: it repeatedly backs out changes that break correctness (data hazards, invalid uniformity check, slot overflows), reverts cleanly to known-working kernels, and updates its machine model when surprised (no intra-cycle forwarding, positional-test constraint). It does not reach 8, however, because it exhibits exactly the sunk-cost persistence and flailing the high anchor rules out: it re-attempts the scratch-heavy sorted-grouping strategy after multiple identical 'out of scratch' failures and oscillates between 2/4-way interleaving without decisively pivoting, while its cost-model estimates keep getting falsified and re-guessed rather than converging. This places observed behavior solidly at the level-5 description with only partial level-8 qualities (precise per-failure diagnosis), netting a 5.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget

evidence.note: Early explicit floor derivation: 512 vectors, per-vector 6 LOAD/19 VALU/2 STORE/4 ALU, bottleneck VALU 19/6=3.17 cyc/vec, theoretical minimum ~1622; recognizes gap to 1250 and pivots to grouping to reduce tree loads.
Detailed per-engine cost model: VALU 15/6=2.5, LOAD 6/2=3, STORE 1, ALU 0.33, FLOW 0; concludes Minimum II=3 → 1536 cycles bounded by LOAD, and computes required II<2.44 to hit 1250.

Uses model to decide transform worth: with grouping LOAD drops to 3.3/vec (845 cyc, achievable) vs without grouping 8/2=4 → 2048 min; concludes grouping is ESSENTIAL to get below 1250 — gap-driven prioritization.
After measuring 5130 then 8018, recomputes bottleneck (tree loads 2048 min vs VALU 1194) and uses it to justify the sorted-grouping direction to cut 4096 tree loads to 667.
Explores an 8-way software-pipeline II=1 model: 512 vectors + ~28 prologue ≈ 540 cycles, tying pipeline depth and slot capacity to a cycle estimate.
Full per-engine cycle accounting with grouping (tree loads 667/2=334, VALU 7680/6=1280, FLOW 1024/1=1024, STORE 512) identifying VALU as new bottleneck — a genuine slot-occupancy lower-bound model.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently built explicit quantitative cost models tying per-vector instruction counts to slot limits (12 ALU/6 VALU/2 LOAD/2 STORE/1 FLOW), derived theoretical lower bounds (~1536-2048 without grouping, ~845-1280 with grouping), and used the measured-vs-floor gap to prioritize which transform (grouping, interleaving, multiply_add/vselect) could actually close the distance to 1250 — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because the floor estimates fluctuated rather than converging to a single tight, stable bound, and the kernel never approached the budget closely enough for the model to identify near-optimality.

rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
